name: North Sikkim: Lachung & Lachen
tagline: Two village councils, two valleys, one sacred lake
meta_description: North Sikkim on a budget: Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar, Lepcha Dzongu. Permits, shared tours from Gangtok, real costs and road status.
summary: North Sikkim is Mangan district: the Lepcha reserve of Dzongu, the Teesta gorge, and the two high valleys of Lachung and Lachen that lead to Yumthang, Zero Point and Gurudongmar Lake. Most visitors join a permit tour from Gangtok; a shared 3-day tour costs about ₹6,000–8,000 per person. Roads close often since 2023: check current status before you travel.

story.title: Where Sikkim's oldest promises were made
paras: Sikkim's own founding story starts here. In the 13th century, the Lepcha chief and seer Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa, a prince from Kham in eastern Tibet, swore blood brotherhood at Kabi Lungchok, 17 km north of present-day Gangtok. Stone pillars still mark the spot. The Bhutia royal line that became the Chogyals of Sikkim in 1642 traced its descent from Khye Bumsa, and the Lepchas, who call themselves Mutanchi Rongkup, held to their place as the first people of the land. Further up the same road, Tumlong served as the Chogyals' capital from 1793 until 1894.

Beyond Mangan the valley splits. At Chungthang the Lachen Chu and the Lachung Chu meet to form the Teesta, and each river leads to a village that runs itself. Lachen, the big pass, and Lachung, the small pass, are governed by the Dzumsa, a council of every household under an elected headman called the Pipon. The system dates from the first half of the 19th century, and the state still recognises it in place of a panchayat. In 1849 the botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker walked up both valleys collecting rhododendrons before he and Archibald Campbell were detained by the Sikkim court.

The north has also lived through hard years. On the night of 3–4 October 2023, South Lhonak lake in the far north-west burst its moraine wall. The flood reached Chungthang around midnight and destroyed the Teesta III dam within minutes, then tore out bridges and stretches of road down the valley. Since then, North Sikkim has opened and closed in stages. Villages that depend on visitors have rebuilt, but every trip here should begin with one question: check current status before you travel.

intro: North Sikkim is the largest district in Sikkim and one of the least populated in India. Officially it has been Mangan district since 2021, named after its headquarters town on the Teesta. In one long day's drive you climb from cardamom groves under 1,000 m at Mangan to apple orchards at Lachung, then on to yak pasture and lakes above 5,000 m near the Tibetan border.

Almost everyone visits on a permit tour sold by registered agents in Gangtok. The classic is 3 days and 2 nights: Lachen and Gurudongmar Lake, then Lachung and Yumthang Valley. You can join a shared vehicle, which keeps the cost per person low, or book a whole car. Indian nationals need a North Sikkim permit; foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit and cannot go to every point.

We also send people to the parts that need no tour at all: Kabi Lungchok, the monasteries of Phodong and Labrang, the Kanchenjunga view at Singhik, and the Lepcha homestays of Dzongu, which need their own permit. Those places run on shared jeeps from Gangtok's Vajra stand and cost a fraction of a package tour. Roads since 2023 change month to month: check current status before you travel.
facts: Gangtok (Vajra stand); NJP / Bagdogra for Gangtok
Mangan ≈ 65 km · 3 h; Lachung ≈ 118 km · 6–8 h
North Sikkim permit for all; PAP for foreigners; separate Dzongu permit

highlights.title: Gurudongmar Lake at dawn
highlights.text: A sacred lake at about 5,180 m, 5 km from the Tibetan border, reached from Lachen by leaving at 3–4 am. Buddhists link it to Guru Padmasambhava. You stay 20–40 minutes, not longer, because of the thin air. Indians only; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Yumthang and its rhododendrons
highlights.text: A grazing valley at 3,564 m, 24 km above Lachung, inside the Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary. From late April to May the slopes turn red, pink and yellow, there is a hot spring by the river, and yaks come up in summer.

highlights.title: The Dzumsa villages
highlights.text: Lachung and Lachen decide their own rules through the Dzumsa, a village council led by the Pipon. Spend an extra night and you see the village itself: Lachung Monastery of 1880, the apple orchards, and the Lachen gompa built in 1858.

highlights.title: Lepcha Dzongu
highlights.text: A reserved Lepcha homeland across the Teesta from Mangan, with its own permit. Stay with a family in Lingthem or Passingdang, eat millet and nettle, and hear how Lepchas see Kanchenjunga as their guardian. Tholung Monastery opens its relics every three years.

highlights.title: Kabi Lungchok and Phodong
highlights.text: Sikkim's history in two short stops within 40 km of Gangtok: the stones of the 13th-century blood-brotherhood oath, then Phodong and Labrang monasteries above the old capital of Tumlong. No permit for Indians, shared jeeps for under ₹200.

highlights.title: Zero Point at Yumesamdong
highlights.text: The end of the civilian road at about 4,700 m, 23 km past Yumthang. Snow lies here well into May, and tea stalls sell Maggi and butter tea in season. It costs extra per vehicle and foreigners are not allowed.

getting_there: Everything starts in Gangtok. From NJP station or Bagdogra airport, shared jeeps to Gangtok leave Siliguri's SNT and Panitanki stands for ₹300–450 a seat and take 4–5 hours on NH10; a reserved car costs ₹3,500–4,500. Pakyong airport near Gangtok has had only patchy flights. North Sikkim tours leave Gangtok around 10–11 am from agents' offices on MG Marg and the Vajra stand, after permits are processed. For Mangan, Singhik, Phodong and Kabi, shared jeeps run from Vajra taxi stand at Maarchak, about 3 km north of the centre, for roughly ₹100–300 a seat. The road north follows the Teesta through landslide country: since the October 2023 flood, closures can last days or weeks. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian nationals need a North Sikkim permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu, Chopta and Gurudongmar. Registered tour operators in Gangtok apply for it; give them a photo ID copy and two photographs a day ahead. Foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit, travel in groups of two or more through a registered agent, and have usually been allowed to Lachung and Yumthang but not to Zero Point or Gurudongmar. Dzongu needs a separate permit for all non-locals, usually issued at Mangan. Rules change: check current status before you travel.
money: A shared 3-day tour from Gangtok to Lachen and Lachung costs about ₹6,000–8,000 per person with permits, rooms and meals. That is the cheapest way north, because tours are priced per vehicle and you are splitting the car. A whole Bolero or Scorpio for the same trip costs roughly ₹18,000–28,000 before hotels. Zero Point adds ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle. People overspend on boots and jackets bought in Gangtok when Lachung rents them for ₹100–300, and on upgrades to hotels they only sleep in. Dzongu homestays run about ₹1,800–2,500 per person with all meals.

months.summary: Deep winter. Lachung and Lachen are snowbound and cold, and Gurudongmar or Zero Point may be cut off for days at a time by fresh snow. When the road holds, January gives clear skies and snow right up to the village. Lower down, Mangan, Singhik and Dzongu are dry and pleasant, with orange season ending. Shared tours run with fewer people, so you may wait a day for a full vehicle.
months.tip: Book a room with a heater or a bukhari stove in Lachung and carry thermal layers.

months.summary: Still winter in the high valleys, with snow at Yumthang and often at Lachung itself. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or early March, and the Bhutia villages mark it at home and at their monasteries. Gurudongmar access is uncertain until the snow eases. The lower villages are good for walking, birds and monasteries without crowds.
months.tip: Ask your agent which high points are open that week before you pay for them.

months.summary: The thaw begins. Yumthang usually reopens and snow still lies in the valley, which is what many Indian families come for. The first rhododendrons flower at lower heights by late March. Days lengthen, and Gurudongmar tours resume as the road clears, though the lake itself stays frozen. Holi week and school holidays bring a rush from the plains, so book early.
months.tip: If you want snow and flowers together, aim for the last ten days of March.

months.summary: Rhododendron month. The Shingba sanctuary around Yumthang begins to flower from the lower slopes up, and Zero Point is still white. Clear mornings are common, afternoons can cloud over with short showers. Tholung Monastery in Dzongu holds its Kamsel relic display in April once every three years. Prices rise with demand from mid-April.
months.tip: Go up to Yumthang early in the day; flowers and peaks are clearest before 11 am.

months.summary: Peak flower season at Yumthang, with primulas following the rhododendrons, and the warmest month to attempt Gurudongmar before the rains. Gurudongmar starts to thaw from mid-May. This is also peak Indian holiday season, so shared tours fill fast and rooms in Lachung are tight. Pre-monsoon storms start in late May; slips on the Teesta road become more likely.
months.tip: Book Lachung rooms and your tour at least two weeks ahead in May.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives and with it the landslide season on the North Sikkim road. Closures that strand travellers in Lachung for days have happened in June more than once. Some tours still run when the road is open, and the high valleys turn green with alpine flowers, but we do not plan trips here in June. Dzongu is wet and leech-heavy.
months.tip: If you must go, keep two buffer days and travel insurance that covers delays.

months.summary: Wettest weeks of the year. The Teesta runs high and brown, slips are frequent, and permits may be suspended at short notice. The upper meadows of Chopta and Yumthang are full of flowers, and yaks graze high, but the drive to reach them is the problem. Prices are lowest. Stay closer to Gangtok, at Kabi and Phodong, if you are in Sikkim now.
months.tip: Watch district administration notices; tours are often cancelled the morning they leave.

months.summary: The monsoon continues. Large cardamom harvest starts in the lower villages around Mangan and Dzongu in late August, and the smell of drying pods reaches the road. Road status is the deciding factor: on a clear week, tours run to Lachung. We still advise against fixed plans this month.
months.tip: Ask in Mangan bazaar about cardamom drying sheds you can visit.

months.summary: The rains thin out through the month and the valleys are at their greenest. Late September often has clear spells, and tours resume more reliably. The October 2023 flood came at the very start of October after extreme rain, so watch the forecast. Rooms are cheaper than in October, and Gurudongmar is unfrozen.
months.tip: Plan for the last week of September and keep the dates flexible.

months.summary: The best all-round month: clear skies, Kanchenjunga visible from Singhik, autumn colour starting in Lachung's maples and larches, and Gurudongmar's water still open. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays bring a wave of Bengali and Indian families, so shared tours and rooms fill early and prices rise for those weeks.
months.tip: Avoid the Puja week itself unless you have booked well ahead.

months.summary: Cold and very clear. Autumn colour peaks in Lachung's valley in early November, Gurudongmar begins to freeze, and the crowds thin after Diwali. Mornings are sharp, especially in Lachen before the Gurudongmar run. Good value: rooms drop back to normal rates and shared tours still fill.
months.tip: Carry a down jacket for the Gurudongmar start at 4 am, when it is well below freezing.

months.summary: Winter sets in, and the first big snow usually reaches Lachung in December or January. Losoong, the Sikkimese harvest new year, is preceded by masked dances at Phodong Monastery. Christmas and New Year weeks are busy with families hoping for snow. Gurudongmar and Zero Point close or open with each snowfall.
months.tip: Fix the Phodong chaam date with the monastery or Sikkim Tourism; it follows the Tibetan calendar.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian nationals need a North Sikkim permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu, Chopta and Gurudongmar, arranged by a registered Gangtok tour operator with a photo ID copy and two photos. Foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit and a registered agent. Dzongu has its own permit. Mangan, Singhik, Phodong and Kabi need none for Indians. Check current status before you travel.

No, not as of our last check. Foreign nationals with a Protected Area Permit have usually been allowed to Lachung and Yumthang, travelling in a group of two or more through a registered agent, but Gurudongmar and Zero Point are closed to them because of their closeness to the border. The list of permitted places changes, so ask the agent and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a North Sikkim tour cost?
faqs.a: A shared 3-day, 2-night tour from Gangtok to Lachen and Lachung costs about ₹6,000–8,000 per person in 2025–26, including permits, a seat in the vehicle, rooms and simple meals. A whole vehicle for the same trip is about ₹18,000–28,000 before hotels. Zero Point costs ₹3,000–4,500 extra per vehicle. Prices rise in May, October and the Christmas weeks.

faqs.q: Is North Sikkim open after the 2023 Teesta flood?
faqs.a: Partly, and it changes. Since the October 2023 flood destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang and many road sections, North Sikkim has reopened in stages, with fresh closures after landslides, especially in the monsoon. Tours to Lachung have run more reliably than to Lachen and Gurudongmar. Check current status before you travel with your agent and the Mangan district administration.

faqs.q: Which is better, Lachung or Lachen?
faqs.a: Do both if you can, because they lead to different things. Lachung, the larger village, is the base for Yumthang Valley and Zero Point and has more rooms and orchards. Lachen is smaller and colder and exists for travellers mainly as the base for Gurudongmar Lake. With only one night, families with small children or older parents often choose Lachung, which avoids the 5,000 m altitude.

faqs.q: Is Gurudongmar safe for children and older people?
faqs.a: It is risky. The lake is at about 5,180 m and you drive up from Lachen, around 2,750 m, in three hours. Headaches, breathlessness and nausea are common. Children under five, people with heart or lung conditions and pregnant women are usually advised not to go. Stay 20–40 minutes, do not run, and turn back if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Three days and two nights from Gangtok covers the classic loop: Lachen, Gurudongmar, Lachung and Yumthang. Four or five nights is better: an extra night at Lachen helps with the altitude, and an extra night at Lachung lets you see the village. Add two or three nights for Dzongu and the Kabi and Phodong stops near Gangtok.

faqs.q: Can I travel to Lachung independently without a tour?
faqs.a: Not really. Permits are issued through registered tour operators, and private cars from outside Sikkim are generally not allowed beyond a point. The practical budget option is a shared tour: you buy a seat in a vehicle that the agent fills. Mangan, Singhik, Phodong and Kabi you can reach on your own by shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra stand.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM in Lachung and Lachen?
faqs.a: Coverage is patchy. BSNL and Jio have usually worked in Lachung and Lachen village, with gaps on the road and at Yumthang and Gurudongmar. Lachung has a State Bank of India branch, and Mangan has several banks, but ATMs can run dry. Carry enough cash from Gangtok for the whole tour plus a margin for delays.
